items: 1908 air burst explosion in Siberia, Russia
books: The Tunguska event was a large explosion that occurred on the morning of 30 June [O.S. 17 June] 1908, at around 7:14 KRAT (0:14 UT) in Central Siberia, then part of the Russian Empire. The cataclysm occurred in a remote and sparsely populated region of the taiga, near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River after which it is named. The shock wave knocked several witnesses to the ground, killed at least three people as well as numerous animals, and shattered windows within a 200 km (120 mi) radius. The blast was recorded by various Russian and German seismological stations with a magnitude close to 5 on the Richter scale, while atmospheric waves generated by the shock wave were detected worldwide. From 30 June to 3 July, intense bright nights were observed across western Eurasia over an area of about 12,000,000 km2 (4,600,000 sq mi).

Although the Siberian press and various correspondents reported the blast in the following days, it was not until 1921 that a first scientific expedition was organized under the direction of Leonid Kulik, who discovered the site of the epicenter only in 1927.
Kulik and his successors' research revealed that the explosion devastated nearly 2,150 km2 (830 sq mi) of forest in a radial pattern which implied an aerial origin. The scientific consensus thus attributes this event to a meteor air burst, the atmospheric explosion of a celestial body, although no fragment has been formally identified. By cross-referencing eyewitness accounts and physical modeling, researchers favor the hypothesis of a 50–60 m (160–200 ft) diameter meteoroid moving at high speed from the south-east. The object would have exploded between 5–10 km (3.1–6.2 mi) in altitude, releasing an energy often estimated between 10 and 15 megatons of TNT, which is enough to destroy an entire major city.
This interpretation is reinforced by data collected since the passage of the Chelyabinsk meteor in 2013, whose dynamics were similar.
